top.title: James Webb reveals a strange bulge in an alien planet's atmosphere
top.summary: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have discovered that a distant alien planet's atmosphere is surprisingly lopsided. Located 1,300 light-years away, the scorching gas giant WASP-17b experiences powerful winds that redistribute heat, causing one side of its atmosphere to bulge outward. A groundbreaking new mapping technique revealed these hidden distortions, confirming predictions about how extreme temperatures and winds shape alien worlds.
top.text: Astronomers have long depicted distant exoplanets with smooth, circular outlines. But new observations reveal that the atmospheres surrounding some of these scorching alien worlds can have surprisingly uneven shapes. Using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), researchers have discovered that the atmosphere of WASP-17b, a giant planet roughly 1,300 light-years from Earth, extends farther outward on one side than the other. Although its overall outline remains approximately circular, its atmosphere is noticeably asymmetrical. The distortion provides new evidence of how extreme temperatures and powerful winds reshape the atmospheres of distant planets. The discovery, published in Nature Astronomy , comes from a study jointly led by Cornell University in the United States and the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom. Researchers used an innovative technique called 'transmission strings', developed by Bristol astrophysicists Dr. David Grant and Dr. Hannah Wakeford, to investigate the planet's atmospheric structure in unprecedented detail. WASP-17b belongs to a class of planets known as 'hot Jupiters', enormous gas giants that orbit close to their host stars and experience intense heating. Its unusual atmospheric shape offers a new perspective on how heat moves around these extreme worlds. Lead author Dr. Lili Alderson, a Klarman Postdoctoral Fellow at Cornell University, began the research while studying at the University of Bristol, where she earned her doctorate in physics. "This is proof of concept that planets are in fact 3D objects, and that consistently, as they go around their star, what we predict should be happening is happening. To move beyond computational exercises and see it for real is a different matter." The observations provide valuable information about WASP-17b's atmospheric chemistry and temperature variations, including differences between its equator and poles and between its permanently illuminated and dark hemispheres. These results closely match earlier theoretical predictions and computer models. Together, they offer one of the most detailed three-dimensional pictures of an exoplanet's atmosphere yet produced, establishing a useful reference point for studying the more than 6,000 exoplanets confirmed so far. Co-author Dr. Hannah Wakeford, Associate Professor in Astrophysics at the University of Bristol, said: "Planets are temperamental, their atmospheres complex and chaotic. The fact that all of these numbers came together and showed us this very structured, dynamical picture of this giant world over 1,000 light-years away was just really exciting." James Webb's extraordinary sensitivity has already enabled scientists to investigate alien atmospheres using a method called eclipse mapping. This approach examines subtle changes in light as a planet moves behind its parent star, helping researchers determine how conditions vary across the planet. The new "transmission strings" technique, also called transit mapping, examines the opposite part of the planet's orbit. As an exoplanet passes in front of its star, some starlight travels through the outer edges of its atmosphere before reaching the telescope. By analyzing that light from different angles, scientists can investigate the atmosphere's composition and determine how far it extends at different locations around the planet. This outer atmospheric boundary is known as the limb. Traditional methods generally combine light measurements from the entire limb into a single average spectrum. The new approach instead separates information from different regions, allowing researchers to identify atmospheric variations that would otherwise be concealed. "Rather than assuming your atmosphere is a circle with the same radius all the way around, our technique allows you to pull out different distances from the center to the edge of the planet," Dr. Alderson said. "We're able to go around the edge. So, we've gone from a ring to understanding where on the ring the gemstones are, so to speak." The new measurements revealed a particularly interesting feature near WASP-17b's equator, precisely where previous models predicted it would appear. The distortion occurs on the planet's "evening" side, where powerful atmospheric winds carry heat away from the hemisphere that permanently faces its star and toward the hemisphere locked in darkness. This movement of hot gas causes the atmosphere on the evening side to expand farther outward than it does on the cooler "morning" side. As a result, the planet's atmospheric outline is not perfectly symmetrical. The findings confirm a major prediction about the temperature differences between these regions. The transit mapping measurements also supported other previously identified characteristics of WASP-17b. Dr. Alderson added: "Theory predicts that the morning and the evening sides should have a strong temperature difference, and WASP-17b fits really nicely in that trend -- pretty much bang-on what we thought it would be." Successfully applying transmission strings to WASP-17b demonstrates that the technique could be used to study the atmospheres of many other exoplanets. Until recently, much of what astronomers could determine about these distant atmospheres came from measurements averaged across large regions. The new method offers a way to distinguish conditions at different latitudes, as well as between the day and night sides of a planet. Eventually, this approach could help scientists investigate atmospheric structures on smaller scales, bringing them closer to mapping weather patterns on worlds far beyond our solar system. Dr. Wakeford said: "Having this very robust mathematical model that we can apply to this state-of-the-art data is incredibly exciting. The results are a really beautiful demonstration of the dynamics that are going on in these multidimensional and multifaceted worlds." The study used observations gathered through JWST's Telescope Scientist Deep Reconnaissance of Exoplanet Atmospheres through Multi-instrument Spectroscopy (TST DREAMS) Guaranteed Time Observations program. top.title: Ozempic and Wegovy linked to rare risk of sudden vision loss
top.summary: Popular diabetes and weight loss drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy have been linked to a slightly increased risk of a rare condition that can cause sudden, potentially permanent vision loss. Although the risk remains very low, Rutgers researchers say the findings warrant attention as millions of people turn to GLP-1 medications.
top.text: A large study led by Rutgers researchers has identified a possible vision risk associated with widely used diabetes and weight loss medications, including Ozempic and Wegovy. The findings suggest that people taking these drugs may face a slightly higher risk of developing a rare eye condition that can cause sudden and potentially permanent vision loss. The condition, known as ischemic optic neuropathy, occurs when blood flow to the optic nerve is reduced. Because the optic nerve carries visual information from the eye to the brain, damage to it can lead to significant vision problems. The study, published in Annals of Internal Medicine , analyzed information from a large database of US adults ages 18 to 65 with Type 2 diabetes. Researchers focused on patients who had recently started taking medications to manage their condition, including a class of drugs known as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, or GLP-1s. These medications include semaglutide (sold as Ozempic and Wegovy) and tirzepatide (sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound). In addition to helping control blood sugar and manage weight, GLP-1 medications can reduce the risks of certain cardiovascular and kidney problems. However, scientists are still investigating their potential side effects as their use becomes increasingly widespread. The researchers found that GLP-1 use was associated with a modest increase in the likelihood of ischemic optic neuropathy. Although the condition was uncommon, its potential consequences make the finding important. "Although ischemic optic neuropathy was rare, it is clinically important because it can involve sudden vision loss," said Chintan Dave, a core faculty member of the Center for Pharmacoepidemiology and Treatment Science at Rutgers Institute for Health, Health Care Policy and Aging Research. "The increase in risk was small -- approximately three to four additional cases per 10,000 patients treated with GLP-1s over 18 months, but clinicians and patients should be aware of this potential association." While the absolute risk remains low, researchers say the growing popularity of GLP-1 medications makes continued safety monitoring especially important. These drugs are now widely prescribed to people both with and without Type 2 diabetes. The study also identified patterns among patients who developed the eye condition. Cases were more common among men and adults in the older portion of the study population. "Most patients in our study who had ischemic optic neuropathy were either men or men and women aged 50 to 65," said Dave, an associate professor at the Ernest Mario School of Pharmacy and the lead author of the study. "Because ischemic optic neuropathy can present with sudden vision loss, which may be permanent, early recognition of symptoms and prompt ophthalmologic evaluation may be especially important for patients at higher baseline risk." More than 80% of ischemic optic neuropathy cases are estimated to involve the non-arteritic anterior form of the condition. This occurs when blood supply to the front portion of the optic nerve becomes insufficient, potentially damaging the nerve and interfering with vision. The resulting vision loss is often permanent. According to Dave, approximately one-third of affected patients experience some recovery, usually during the first six months. Even when improvement occurs, some degree of visual impairment typically remains. Rather than causing complete blindness, the condition usually affects part of the vision in one eye. Patients may notice sudden blurriness, dimming, or missing areas in their field of view. Despite the association, the researchers caution that their findings do not establish that GLP-1 medications directly cause optic nerve damage. Other factors, including differences in patients' underlying health conditions, could help explain the increased risk observed in the study. Additional research will be necessary to determine whether the medications themselves contribute to the condition. For now, the findings highlight the importance of recognizing sudden vision changes and seeking prompt medical evaluation, particularly among people who may already be at greater risk. The research team also included Kamika Reynolds and Kimberly O'Malley of the Institute for Health, along with Jason Roy of the Rutgers School of Public Health. top.title: NASA’s Curiosity rover reveals a spectacular new view of Mars with a mystery on the horizon
top.summary: NASA’s Curiosity rover has revealed a spectacular new view of mysterious, wind-carved cliffs on Mars that may hold evidence of ancient volcanic activity. With the rover approaching these unusual formations, scientists hope to uncover the secrets behind their strange appearance in 2027.
top.text: NASA's Curiosity rover has captured a spectacular new panorama of Mars, providing its clearest look yet at a series of mysterious cliffs shaped by wind. Scientists have been eager to examine these distant formations up close, and the latest images offer an exciting preview of what lies ahead. Taken at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, the scene reveals striking blue tones across the foreground while morning sunlight illuminates rugged cliffs known as yardangs along the horizon. Curiosity recorded the panorama using its Mastcam on August 11, during the mission's 4,982nd Martian day, or sol. Six separate photographs were transmitted to Earth and combined to create the sweeping view. Unlike most Mastcam photographs, the images were processed without white balancing, allowing the scene to retain the distinctive colors and lighting of the Martian morning. The yardangs stretch approximately 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern portion of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been climbing since 2014. The rover recently achieved a major milestone, gaining 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) in elevation, a greater climb than any other rover has completed on Mars. As Curiosity continues toward these unusual formations, researchers anticipate increasingly detailed views of the cliffs. More importantly, they hope that examining the rocks firsthand will help explain how the remarkable landscape developed. Mount Sharp contains numerous layers of sedimentary rock, each preserving evidence from a different chapter of Martian history. Investigating these layers has helped scientists reconstruct a time billions of years ago when lakes and streams existed in this region of Mars. As the planet's environment changed, those bodies of water eventually disappeared, leaving deposits of salty minerals behind. Once additional material stopped accumulating on the mountain, powerful winds may have gradually eroded portions of the existing rock, carving out the distinctive yardangs visible today. Yet the unusual appearance of this particular layer has raised questions about its origins. Its color differs from the surrounding terrain, and its rock layers are tilted in an unexpected direction. Scientists suspect that processes beyond ordinary wind erosion may have contributed to its formation. "The yardang layer looks out of place. It's the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on," said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "But that's what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions." Curiosity is now in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which began with an investigation of unusual spiderweb-like boxwork ridges. Over roughly the next year, the rover will continue traveling through rock layers containing abundant sulfates and carbonates, minerals that provide evidence of ancient drying conditions on Mars. Mission scientists aim to reach the bottom of the yardang formations sometime in 2027. Once there, Curiosity should be able to examine the mysterious cliffs using its robotic arm, gathering unique measurements that could help determine how they formed and reveal more about the environmental changes that shaped Mars billions of years ago. top.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between vitamin C and cancer survival
top.summary: A surprising clinical trial suggests that taking vitamin C daily could improve survival in people with precancerous blood disorders and early-stage blood cancers. Patients receiving the supplement had fewer adverse events and showed a promising survival advantage, raising hopes that a common vitamin could help protect against leukemia-related complications.
top.text: Vitamin C plays an important role in keeping the immune system healthy, helping wounds heal, and protecting cells from damage. However, people with precancerous blood disorders and blood cancers often have persistently low vitamin C levels. Researchers have been investigating whether correcting this deficiency could improve their health and treatment outcomes. New findings from the phase 2 EVITA clinical trial suggest that vitamin C supplementation may offer important benefits for people with precancerous blood conditions and early-stage blood cancers. The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study was conducted by the Van Andel Institute-Stand Up To Cancer® Epigenetics Dream Team. The results, published in the American Cancer Society journal CANCER , revealed that patients who received 1,000 mg of oral vitamin C every day for one year experienced fewer adverse events during the study and its follow-up period. The supplement also changed the levels of certain immune signaling molecules, known as cytokines, in ways associated with more favorable outcomes. These changes suggest that vitamin C could influence inflammation-related processes involved in the growth and progression of abnormal blood cells. Although vitamin C did not significantly affect the rate at which abnormal blood cells expanded, the researchers identified an encouraging result. An exploratory analysis showed that participants who received vitamin C were significantly more likely to be alive after approximately three years of follow-up than those who took a placebo. Scientists emphasize that this potential survival benefit must be verified in a larger phase 3 clinical trial. "We are tremendously excited and cautiously optimistic that our results could one day translate into a simple way to improve care and outcomes for people with pre-leukemia disorders," said Peter A. Jones, Ph.D., D.Sc. (hon), a distinguished professor at Van Andel Institute. Jones is also a co-corresponding author of the research and co-leader of the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team. "Our approach reflects a growing emphasis on cancer interception -- intervening before cancer becomes established. We are working to build on the trial findings by exploring how exactly vitamin C interacts with pre-cancerous cells, including the idea that it may help restore normal epigenetic function in blood cells at risk of becoming leukemia." The international research effort was led by Kirsten Grønbæk, M.D., Ph.D., a leading hematologist, professor at the University of Copenhagen, and member of the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team. "These exciting preliminary findings lay the groundwork for a larger clinical trial to explore vitamin C as a possible way to improve patient outcomes," said Grønbæk. "It is too early to make definitive recommendations based on our results, but we are hopeful that a more expansive study will provide further insights." First Clinical Trial Tests Daily Vitamin C for Precancerous Blood Disorders The study enrolled 109 patients with either clonal cytopenia of undetermined significance (CCUS) or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). Both conditions can develop into acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive form of blood cancer that is often difficult to treat. The likelihood of developing CCUS and related blood disorders rises with age, making these conditions particularly common among older adults. Currently, no approved treatment can prevent CCUS from progressing to leukemia. Although stem cell transplantation is an option for treating MDS, many patients cannot undergo the procedure because of age or other medical conditions. None of the people enrolled in the trial were receiving cancer treatment when the study took place. To determine whether vitamin C might offer benefits, researchers randomly divided participants into two groups. One received 1,000 mg of vitamin C by mouth each day for 12 months. The other received a placebo designed to be indistinguishable from the supplement in appearance, taste, and smell, but containing no vitamin C. Neither the participants nor the clinical staff knew who was receiving vitamin C until the study concluded. This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled approach is considered the gold standard in clinical research because it reduces potential bias and allows investigators to assess treatment effects more objectively. The research was carried out at four hospitals: Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen University Hospital-Herlev, Aalborg University Hospital, and Keck Hospital of the University of Southern California. What makes EVITA particularly notable is that it was the first randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to investigate oral vitamin C in patients with conditions that can precede leukemia or with lower-risk myeloid cancers. Earlier studies had primarily examined vitamin C administered intravenously and had focused on solid tumors rather than precancerous blood disorders or early-stage blood malignancies. EVITA instead evaluated a daily oral dose comparable to that available in many over-the-counter vitamin C supplements. Blood samples collected throughout the study allowed researchers to track participants' vitamin C concentrations and determine whether supplementation corrected deficiencies. At the beginning of the trial, more than half of the participants had insufficient vitamin C levels. Among those assigned to the supplementation group, blood concentrations returned to normal after they began taking vitamin C. For patients living with conditions that could eventually develop into leukemia, the possibility of an accessible intervention is especially important. In many cases, physicians have little choice but to monitor the disease and watch for signs that it is progressing. "The standard approach for patients with pre-cancer blood disorders is to monitor their blood cell counts over time. This is, understandably, very frustrating -- no one wants to hear that they have a condition that increases leukemia risk but there's nothing that can be done other than watch and wait," said Casey O'Connell, M.D., FACP, the Lawrence and Jane Kelly Chair in Hematology at the University of Southern California and lead clinician at USC's trial location. "The EVITA trial took on this challenge by exploring vitamin C's potential to address the underlying factors that drive leukemia development." Scientists have investigated whether vitamin C could play a useful role in cancer treatment for more than seven decades. For much of that time, the evidence remained uncertain because studies produced inconsistent findings and employed different experimental methods. During the past decade, however, improved research technologies have revealed that vitamin C has important functions beyond its familiar roles in nutrition and immunity. In particular, scientists have uncovered its involvement in controlling gene activity and guiding normal cell development. One of the most important discoveries concerns TET2, an enzyme that helps prevent cancerous growth by controlling whether particular genes are switched "on" or "off." Vitamin C supports the activity of this enzyme, which helps maintain normal patterns of gene regulation. Mutations affecting TET2 are frequently found in leukemia and related blood disorders. When the enzyme's normal function is disrupted, abnormal cells can gain an opportunity to multiply and potentially develop into cancer. Experiments using cancer models have provided additional evidence of vitamin C's possible protective effects. These studies found that supplementation could interfere with cellular changes associated with cancer and slow the progression of leukemia. Notably, the strongest effects appeared when vitamin C was introduced before cancer had become established. top.title: NASA solves a strange mystery hidden inside asteroid Bennu’s boulders
top.summary: NASA scientists have finally uncovered why asteroid Bennu loses heat so quickly despite being covered in massive boulders. Samples returned to Earth reveal that its rocks are filled with hidden cracks, solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for years.
top.text: NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission encountered an unexpected mystery when it arrived at asteroid Bennu in 2018. Instead of the relatively smooth terrain that earlier observations had suggested, the spacecraft found a rugged landscape dominated by enormous boulders, with very few areas suitable for collecting samples. "When OSIRIS-REx got to Bennu in 2018, we were surprised by what we saw," said Andrew Ryan, a scientist at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory, who led the mission's working group responsible for analyzing the physical and thermal properties of its samples. "We expected some boulders, but we anticipated at least some large regions with smoother, finer regolith that would be easy to collect. Instead, it looked like it was all boulders, and we were scratching our heads for a while." The discovery was especially confusing because of what astronomers had previously learned about Bennu's ability to retain heat. Measurements from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope in 2007 indicated that the asteroid's surface warmed and cooled rapidly as it rotated through sunlight and darkness. Scientists describe this property as low thermal inertia. Materials with low thermal inertia, such as beach sand, quickly gain heat in sunlight and lose it once the Sun disappears. Large, solid rocks behave differently. Much like concrete, they typically hold on to warmth and release it gradually. Bennu's boulder-covered surface appeared to contradict those earlier measurements, leaving researchers with a puzzling question: How could an asteroid covered in massive rocks cool so quickly? Observations collected by OSIRIS-REx while surveying Bennu offered an early clue. The asteroid's boulders might contain far more empty space than scientists had assumed, allowing them to lose heat faster than ordinary solid rocks. When samples from Bennu were returned to Earth, researchers finally had an opportunity to examine that possibility directly. Ryan and his colleagues used several laboratory techniques to investigate tiny rock fragments collected from the asteroid. Their findings, published in Nature Communications , confirmed that the rocks were indeed highly porous. However, porosity alone could not fully explain Bennu's unusually rapid heat loss. The researchers discovered another important feature. Many of the rock particles contained extensive networks of cracks running through their interiors. To investigate how these fractures influence the movement of heat, researchers at Nagoya University in Japan examined the samples using a technique called lock-in thermography. This method uses a laser to heat a tiny area of a sample while measuring how the heat spreads through the surrounding material, much like ripples expanding across the surface of a pond. "That's when things became really interesting," Ryan said. "The thermal inertia measured in the lab samples turned out to be much higher than what the spacecraft's instruments had recorded, echoing similar findings obtained by the team of OSIRIS-REx's partner mission, JAXA's (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) Hayabusa-2." The difference between laboratory measurements and spacecraft observations suggested that the size and internal structure of Bennu's rocks were essential to understanding their behavior. Because the returned samples were much smaller than the enormous boulders covering Bennu, scientists needed a way to determine how heat would move through the material on a much larger scale. At NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, researchers prepared the samples for detailed X-ray imaging while taking special precautions to prevent contamination. Inside a glove box filled with protective nitrogen gas, team members sealed individual rock particles in airtight containers. They then transported the containers to a laboratory for X-ray computed tomography, or XCT scanning. After imaging, the particles were returned to the glove box without being exposed to Earth's environment. "The sample goes into its own 'spacesuit,' gets a CT scan, and then comes back to its pristine environment, all without having any exposure to the terrestrial environment," said Nicole Lunning, lead OSIRIS-REx sample curator within the Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science division at NASA Johnson and one of the study's co-authors. "We can image right through these airtight containers to visualize the shape and internal structure of the rock that's inside." The scans gave scientists a detailed view of the samples' interiors, revealing structures that could not be examined simply by looking at their surfaces. "X-ray computed tomography allows us to look at the inside of an object in three dimensions, without damaging it," said study co-author and NASA Johnson X-ray scientist Scott Eckley. Each scan also produced a permanent three-dimensional digital record of the particle's exterior and internal features. These records were added to a publicly accessible database, allowing the samples to be studied without repeatedly handling the original material. Ryan's team then incorporated the X-ray scan data into computer simulations designed to track how heat travels through asteroid rocks. By extending the calculations from individual particles to the much larger boulders found on Bennu, they were able to reproduce the low thermal inertia observed by the spacecraft. The results resolved a key mystery about Bennu's unusual surface. Scientists had previously considered whether the asteroid's boulders might be extremely porous, with a soft, fluffy, or even sponge-like internal structure. Although the rocks do contain substantial pore space, the researchers found that their widespread internal fractures were equally important to understanding how they retain and release heat. "It turns out that they're really cracked too, and that was the missing piece of the puzzle," Ryan said. The discovery has implications beyond Bennu. Astronomers frequently rely on measurements of how an asteroid absorbs and releases heat to estimate the physical properties of its surface. Until now, interpreting those observations has been difficult without actual rock samples to examine. Ron Ballouz, a scientist at the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory in Laurel, Maryland, and the study's second author, explained that the findings provide a valuable connection between measurements made remotely and the true internal structure of asteroid material. "We can finally ground our understanding of telescope observations of the thermal properties of an asteroid through analyzing these samples from that very same asteroid," Ballouz said. top.title: Rare study reveals a striking divide inside an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain
top.summary: A rare examination of an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain revealed that regions cleared of amyloid plaques had remarkably little of the harmful tau buildup associated with memory loss, while neighboring areas showed extensive damage. The discovery suggests that removing amyloid may have lasting protective effects and could help slow Alzheimer’s progression, especially when treatment begins early.
top.text: An unusually detailed examination of an Alzheimer's patient's brain has revealed striking differences between regions where treatment successfully removed harmful amyloid plaques and areas where those plaques remained. The regions cleared of amyloid showed little or no buildup of tau tangles, another protein abnormality strongly associated with brain cell damage and declining memory. Nearby areas that still contained amyloid, however, showed much higher levels of tau and evidence of continued neurodegeneration. The discovery offers rare evidence from a human brain that removing amyloid plaques may provide protection against other damaging processes involved in Alzheimer's disease (AD). The results also suggest that clearing amyloid thoroughly, particularly early in the disease, could help limit tau accumulation and slow the progression of brain damage. Researchers from the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania presented the findings at the 2026 Alzheimer's Association International Conference. The study was also published in JAMA . "Seeing both disease patterns side-by-side in the same brain gave us a rare opportunity to understand how amyloid removal affects other proteins that contribute to Alzheimer's disease," said co-senior author David Wolk, MD, co-director of the Penn Memory Center and director of the Penn Alzheimer's Disease Research Center. "The findings provide some of the clearest human evidence to date that anti-amyloid therapies may limit the accumulation of tau and slow the brain changes that lead to memory loss and cognitive decline." Two proteins play major roles in the development of Alzheimer's disease. Beta-amyloid collects outside nerve cells, forming sticky deposits known as plaques. Tau, meanwhile, accumulates inside neurons and forms abnormal tangles. Both are associated with the progressive damage to brain cells that contributes to memory problems, changes in personality, and difficulties with thinking. Treatments designed to eliminate amyloid plaques have significantly changed how Alzheimer's is managed in recent years. Aducanumab became the first drug of this type to receive accelerated approval from the FDA, although it is no longer sold. Since then, newer and more effective medications that target amyloid through a similar approach, donanemab (Kisunla) and lecanemab (Leqembi), have received full FDA approval. Researchers have long believed that amyloid buildup helps create the conditions in which harmful tau tangles develop. What has been much harder to establish is whether eliminating amyloid can also limit tau accumulation in the human brain. Direct evidence has been scarce because relatively few people who received amyloid-clearing drugs have undergone brain examinations after death. The researchers were able to investigate this question using brain tissue donated by a former Alzheimer's clinical trial participant. The man was in his fifties when he was diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment caused by Alzheimer's disease. He subsequently joined a clinical trial testing aducanumab and received 30 doses of the medication over four and a half years. He died approximately four years after his last dose, more than a decade after his first symptoms appeared. Before his death, he expressed a wish to donate his brain to scientific research. The tissue was provided to the Center for Neurodegenerative Disease Research in the Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine. When specialists examined the donated brain, they discovered an unusual pattern in which neighboring regions showed dramatically different amounts of Alzheimer's-related damage. The raised ridges of the brain's folded surface, known as gyri, had lost most of their amyloid plaques and contained very little accumulated tau. In contrast, the neighboring grooves between these ridges, called sulci, still contained considerable amyloid buildup. These regions also exhibited substantially more tau tangles, inflammation, and degeneration of brain tissue. This patchwork distribution was consistent with scans taken while the patient was alive, which had already indicated that amyloid removal varied considerably across different parts of his brain. "Many previous reports have shown either extensive amyloid clearance or limited clearance," said co-senior author Edward B. Lee, MD, PhD, the John Q. Trojanowski, MD, PhD Professor for Neurodegenerative Disease Research in Pathology and Laboratory Medicine. "This case represented a unique 'Goldilocks' scenario in which some regions cleared amyloid and others did not. It allowed us to directly compare what happened next in neighboring brain regions and better understand the relationship between amyloid, tau, and neurodegeneration." The findings could have important implications for the latest generation of Alzheimer's medications, which remove amyloid using mechanisms similar to the therapy received by this patient. Although the investigation involved only one individual, the contrast between different brain regions suggests that substantial amyloid removal may influence other disease processes long after treatment has stopped. The results also raise an important question about how the benefits of Alzheimer's drugs are measured. Clinical trials commonly evaluate patients over approximately 18 months, but some protective effects might take considerably longer to become apparent. However, the study cannot establish how much amyloid must be removed to achieve lasting protection or prove that plaque clearance was directly responsible for the differences in tau accumulation and brain damage. Researchers now hope to understand why certain parts of the brain respond more effectively to amyloid-clearing treatments than others. Identifying and potentially strengthening the biological mechanisms responsible for plaque removal could lead to better therapies. Another major question is whether beginning treatment before extensive tau tangles develop could substantially delay Alzheimer's or even prevent the disease from emerging. Because amyloid can accumulate silently in the brain for many years before memory problems begin, researchers are increasingly interested in treating people during the earliest stages of the disease, potentially before noticeable symptoms appear. "Patients may accumulate amyloid for years before symptoms appear," said first author Christopher A. Brown, MD, PhD, an assistant professor of Neurology. "This case suggests that removing amyloid early may help limit the changes that ultimately damage brain cells. Ongoing trials will help determine whether starting treatment before symptoms begin can provide even greater benefit." top.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
top.summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.
top.text: Plastic pollution is one of the world's most persistent environmental problems. Vast amounts of discarded plastic accumulate in the oceans, sometimes forming enormous garbage patches that threaten marine life. Most conventional plastics break down extremely slowly because microorganisms struggle to digest the synthetic polymers from which they are made. Instead of disappearing, these materials gradually fragment into increasingly smaller particles, including microplastics and nanoplastics. Yet plastic waste is not completely beyond the reach of nature. Bacteria and other microorganisms can colonize its surfaces, forming communities known as biofilms. These communities create a distinctive microbial ecosystem that scientists call the "plastisphere." Researchers at the University of Konstanz have now discovered an unusual enzyme that could reveal how some bacteria are becoming better equipped to break down certain types of plastic. The enzyme can digest particular polyesters and biodegradable plastics, but it has another unexpected ability: it can also break down penicillin, suggesting a possible connection to antibiotic resistance. Scientists have nicknamed it the "Pac-Man enzyme" because its molecular structure features a remarkably wide opening where chemical reactions take place, known as the active site. The discovery suggests that bacteria may be adapting to digest certain plastic materials more quickly than researchers previously believed. However, the findings also highlight an important limitation. For microorganisms to make a meaningful difference in reducing plastic pollution, more plastic products would need to be made from biodegradable materials that contain chemical bonds microbes can break apart. To investigate how microorganisms digest biodegradable plastics, University of Konstanz biologists Harry Lerner and David Schleheck studied the entire process of microbial decomposition. They wanted to determine not only whether the materials could be completely broken down, but also which microorganisms were responsible and what biological mechanisms allowed them to do it. The researchers examined the composition of the microbial communities involved and analyzed their collective genetic information (the metagenome). This approach allowed them to search for genes that might produce enzymes capable of breaking apart plastic polymers. Their experiments focused on long-chain aliphatic polyesters (LCAP), a class of biodegradable plastic materials developed by a research team led by chemist Stefan Mecking. These materials contain chemical bonds that certain microorganisms can potentially break down, unlike the more resistant structures found in many conventional plastics. The collaborative findings were published in The ISME Journal . To observe how the bioplastics behaved in a natural environment, the team placed samples beneath the surface of forest soil at the university's botanical garden. "We buried small pieces of LCAP bioplastic film in the upper humus layer in the forest at the university's botanical garden, about ten centimeters deep," explains Harry Lerner. "This layer is where the breakdown of cellulose and other natural polymers, such as cutin - a plant-based polyester - takes place." Humus is the upper layer of soil rich in decomposing organic matter, where microorganisms play a major role in recycling nutrients. Cellulose is the main structural component of plant cell walls, while cutin is a naturally occurring polyester that helps form the protective outer covering of plants. The researchers selected this environment because its microorganisms already possess the biological machinery needed to break down complex natural materials. Alongside the outdoor experiment, the scientists carried out laboratory tests using soil collected from the same forest. They mixed powdered bioplastics into the soil and monitored microbial activity over the course of an entire year. One important measurement was the amount of carbon dioxide, or CO2, released from the samples. As microorganisms consume and metabolize organic materials, they produce carbon dioxide through respiration. Tracking this gas helped the researchers determine how actively the microbes were breaking down the plastics. The buried plastic films remained in the forest soil for a full year, allowing the team to compare decomposition under natural conditions with the carefully monitored laboratory experiments. To assess the results, the scientists also tested cellulose, other biodegradable plastics, conventional polyethylene plastic, and soil samples without added materials. "Cellulose, other types of bioplastics such as PHBV and PCL, as well as high-density plastic (HDPE) and untreated soil were used as controls in the laboratory. We found that all bioplastic materials were completely degraded within roughly 250 to 330 days. Cellulose broke down after about 80 days, whereas virtually no degradation occurred for HDPE," says Lerner. The difference was striking. While the biodegradable plastics were completely broken down within approximately nine to eleven months, conventional high-density polyethylene showed almost no decomposition. These results demonstrate why the chemical makeup of plastic matters so much. Some polymers contain bonds that microbial enzymes can attack, allowing bacteria to dismantle them into smaller molecules. Others, including widely used polyethylene, are far more resistant to biological degradation. When the researchers recovered the plastic films from the forest soil, they discovered something unexpected. Using electron microscopy, which can reveal structures far too small to see with an ordinary light microscope, the team examined the surfaces of the buried materials. They found numerous tiny holes, each approximately matching the dimensions and shape of an individual bacterial cell. The unusual pattern suggested that bacteria were doing more than simply attaching themselves to the plastic. They appeared to be breaking into the material itself. "We hypothesized that bacteria are coated with plastic-depolymerases anchored to their cell surfaces. This would enable them to digest their way into the material and become embedded within the film, leaving behind microscopic holes of exactly this type," explains Lerner. Depolymerases are enzymes that break large molecules called polymers into smaller chemical units. If these enzymes are attached directly to the outside of a bacterium, they could allow the microorganism to digest the surrounding material while remaining in close contact with it. This would help explain the microscopic cavities observed in the plastic films. Rather than relying entirely on enzymes released into the environment, the bacteria might be able to break down the material directly at their surfaces. To find the biological machinery behind this unusual behavior, Lerner extracted DNA from the entire community of microorganisms living in the soil samples. He then sequenced the genetic material and carefully analyzed the extensive data to determine which microbes and genes became especially abundant as the bioplastics decomposed. One gene stood out. It was strongly enriched specifically in forest soil containing LCAP, suggesting that it could play an important role in breaking down the biodegradable polyester. Further analysis revealed that the gene produces an esterase, a type of enzyme capable of splitting certain chemical bonds found in esters. These bonds are present in many naturally occurring substances as well as in various biodegradable polyesters. What made this particular enzyme especially interesting was how it was positioned on bacterial cells. top.title: Music can enhance the flavor of your food
top.summary: The moment we take a sip of our morning coffee or our first bite of lunch, the brain begins interpreting what we taste. Is it sweet? Sour? Or something else entirely? But the brain does not create flavor based solely on signals from the tongue. That is the finding of a new study from the Department of Food Science, published in Scientific Reports.

top.title: Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
top.summary: Even under general anesthesia, the human brain can analyze language, recognize different types of words, and predict what comes next in a story, according to a surprising discovery by Baylor researchers. The findings challenge our understanding of consciousness and suggest that the unconscious brain is far more capable than scientists previously realized.
top.text: Even when a person is fully unconscious under general anesthesia, their brain may still be doing something remarkable: processing language, recognizing patterns, and even anticipating which words will come next. Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine have discovered that the brain retains surprisingly sophisticated abilities during anesthesia, despite the absence of conscious awareness. The findings, published in the journal Nature , challenge traditional assumptions about the relationship between consciousness and thinking. They could also provide new insights into how the brain processes memories and language, potentially leading to advances in technologies that help people communicate after neurological injuries. "Our findings show that the brain is far more active and capable during unconsciousness than previously thought," said Dr. Sameer Sheth, professor and Cullen Foundation Endowed chair of neurosurgery and a McNair Scholar at Baylor. "Even when patients are fully anesthetized, their brains continue to analyze the world around them." To investigate what happens inside the unconscious brain, Sheth, who is also a neurosurgeon at Baylor St. Luke's Medical Center, and his colleagues studied patients undergoing epilepsy surgery while under general anesthesia. These procedures offered an unusual opportunity to examine the hippocampus, a brain structure deeply involved in learning and memory. Located within the brain's temporal lobe, the hippocampus helps organize information and plays an important role in forming new memories. The researchers used advanced recording devices called Neuropixels probes to monitor electrical signals from hundreds of individual neurons in the hippocampus. These tiny probes can detect activity from many nerve cells simultaneously, providing a detailed picture of how groups of neurons respond to information. According to the researchers, this technology had not previously been used to investigate this particular brain region in this way. It allowed the team to examine how the hippocampus responds to sounds and language while patients are unconscious and unable to report what they experience. The first experiment involved playing a series of repeating tones, occasionally interrupted by a sound that differed from the others. Although the patients were under anesthesia, neurons in their hippocampus responded differently to the unexpected sounds. Even more surprisingly, the brain cells became better at distinguishing these unusual tones as the experiment continued. This improvement suggested that the hippocampus was showing signs of neural plasticity, the brain's ability to change its responses through experience. In other words, some of the basic processes associated with learning appeared to remain active even without conscious awareness. The researchers then tested whether the unconscious brain could handle something more complicated than simple sounds. They played short stories to the anesthetized patients while continuing to record activity from neurons in the hippocampus. The results revealed a surprising level of language processing. Distinct patterns of neural activity contained information about different categories of words, including nouns, verbs, and adjectives. This suggested that the hippocampus was responding to meaningful features of language rather than simply detecting that sounds were occurring. The researchers found that neural activity also carried information that could be used to predict upcoming words in a sentence. Even though the patients were unconscious, their brains appeared to anticipate how the language unfolding around them might continue. "The brain appears to anticipate what comes next in a story, even without conscious awareness," said Sheth, who is also Director of The Gordon and Mary Cain Pediatric Neurology Research Foundation Laboratories within the Duncan Neurological Research Institute at Texas Children's Hospital. This ability is related to a process known as predictive coding. Rather than passively receiving information, the brain continually uses patterns and previous experience to anticipate what might happen next. When listening to someone speak, for example, the brain can use the words already heard to form expectations about what is likely to follow. Scientists have typically studied this kind of sophisticated prediction in people who are awake and paying attention. Finding evidence of it during general anesthesia suggests that at least some of the underlying neural processes can operate independently of conscious awareness. "This kind of predictive coding is something we associate with being awake and attentive, yet it's happening here in an unconscious state," said Dr. Benjamin Hayden, professor of neurosurgery at Baylor. The findings raise important questions about what consciousness actually contributes to the brain's ability to process information. Consciousness is generally associated with subjective awareness, including the experience of hearing, thinking, and understanding the world around us. Yet the study suggests that some neural processes involved in interpreting language and predicting future information can continue even when that awareness is absent. This does not necessarily mean that the anesthetized patients consciously understood the stories being played to them. Instead, it indicates that the brain can carry out surprisingly complex aspects of language processing without a person being aware of doing so. The distinction could help researchers better understand how consciousness emerges. One possibility is that awareness depends not simply on whether individual brain regions remain active, but on how information is coordinated and shared across larger networks of brain regions. Under this view, a structure such as the hippocampus might continue analyzing information even when the broader communication between brain regions needed for conscious experience is disrupted. A Surprising Connection Between the Brain and Artificial Intelligence The discovery also highlights an intriguing similarity between human brain activity and artificial intelligence (AI). Large language models, the technology behind many modern AI chatbots, generate text by using patterns learned from enormous amounts of language data to predict what should come next. The researchers observed a related predictive ability in the hippocampus, where neural signals reflected information about upcoming words even during unconsciousness. Although biological brains and AI models operate in fundamentally different ways, both can use patterns in language to anticipate future information. Studying these similarities may help scientists better understand how prediction works in natural and artificial systems. The findings could also have practical implications for brain-computer interfaces, which use signals recorded from the brain to communicate with external devices. One potential application involves speech prosthetics, technologies designed to help people communicate when injuries or neurological conditions have impaired their ability to speak. If scientists can reliably identify meaningful language signals in the brain, those signals might eventually be used to support communication technologies for patients who have lost speech abilities. "Can we use these signals to deploy and run a speech prosthetic for some of the parts of the brain that are damaged by stroke or injury? These are questions that we can now consider in relation to this part of the brain," said Dr. Vigi Katlowitz, first author and a neurosurgery resident with Baylor. top.title: Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger
top.summary: Yale scientists have uncovered how the stress hormone cortisol helps the brain turn emotional experiences into stronger, longer-lasting memories. The discovery reveals that stress can reshape communication between brain networks involved in emotion and memory, potentially explaining why certain moments are so difficult to forget.
top.text: Stress does more than influence how we feel. It can also change what we remember, particularly when an experience is emotionally intense or personally meaningful. Scientists have long known that cortisol, a hormone released during stressful situations, can strengthen emotional memories. What has been less clear is exactly how this happens inside the brain. Researchers at Yale University have now uncovered important clues. Their study reveals that cortisol strengthens emotional memories by changing how brain networks involved in emotion and memory function and communicate with one another. The findings offer a deeper understanding of why certain experiences leave such powerful impressions while others quickly fade. "We all experience stress, and my lab is interested in understanding how stress can be helpful," said corresponding author Elizabeth Goldfarb, an assistant professor of psychiatry at Yale School of Medicine and of psychology in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences. The findings were published in the journal Science Advances . Previous research involving both humans and rodents has shown that stress and cortisol can improve memory for emotional events. Scientists also know that certain brain regions, including the amygdala, play an essential role in this process. The amygdala is particularly important for processing emotions and identifying experiences that may be significant. However, understanding precisely how cortisol strengthens memories has been challenging. Many brain regions participate in several mental functions, making it difficult to determine whether the hormone is influencing emotional responses, memory formation, or both. "Forming memories for emotional experiences involves different processes in the brain: first, perceiving an experience as emotional or intense, and second, encoding that experience into long-term memory," said Goldfarb, who is also a member of Yale's Wu Tsai Institute, an interdisciplinary research initiative that explores cognition. The researchers wanted to examine these processes separately to determine how cortisol affects the brain's ability to recognize emotional significance and preserve an experience as a lasting memory. To investigate, the Yale team conducted an experiment in which participants took a pill containing either hydrocortisone, a form of cortisol, or an inactive placebo. They then viewed a series of pictures while undergoing functional MRI (fMRI) scanning. This imaging technique measures changes in blood flow and oxygen levels associated with brain activity, allowing researchers to identify which areas of the brain are more active during different tasks. As participants examined the pictures, they reported their emotional reactions to each image. The following day, researchers tested how well they remembered what they had seen. Each person completed the experiment twice, once after receiving hydrocortisone and once after receiving the placebo. The study used a double blind design, meaning neither the participants nor the experimenter knew which substance had been administered during a particular session. This approach allowed the scientists to compare how the same person's brain responded with and without the additional cortisol. One of the study's most important advances came from the way researchers analyzed the brain scans. Scientists often study a measurement called functional connectivity, which describes how closely activity in different parts of the brain fluctuates together. When two regions show synchronized patterns of activity, it can indicate that they are participating in related processes. Traditionally, examining these relationships requires several minutes of brain imaging data. The Yale team instead analyzed functional connectivity during individual trials lasting only around five seconds. Using these brief snapshots, the researchers tested whether patterns of brain activity could predict two different outcomes: how emotionally intense participants found a picture and whether they would remember that picture the following day. The approach worked for both. By identifying patterns associated with emotional intensity and memory formation separately, the scientists were able to examine how cortisol influenced each network and the interactions between them. This gave the researchers a more detailed picture of the changing brain activity associated with emotional memory formation. First, cortisol improved participants' ability to remember emotionally significant experiences, confirming what earlier research had suggested. Second, and more importantly, the hormone strengthened emotional memory through distinct changes in the brain networks responsible for processing emotion and forming memories. In networks associated with emotion, cortisol produced more consistent patterns of activity and increased their engagement. This suggests that the hormone helped the brain respond more strongly and reliably to the emotional significance of an experience. In memory networks, cortisol had a different effect. It made their activity patterns more specialized for emotional information, suggesting that the brain was adjusting how it encoded emotionally meaningful experiences. The hormone also increased coordination between the networks involved in emotion and memory. In other words, cortisol appeared to help these different brain systems work together more effectively when processing experiences that carried emotional weight. Together, these findings suggest that stress strengthens emotional memories through several interacting brain mechanisms rather than through a single region or process. The results help explain why stress does not necessarily improve memory for everything. Instead, its benefits appear to be selective, making experiences that feel particularly intense or meaningful more likely to be remembered. The researchers believe this reflects the brain's ability to adapt to stressful situations by prioritizing information that may be important. "Stress responses are fundamentally adaptive and can help you form strong memories -- but this is specific to experiences that you find to be emotionally intense or meaningful," Goldfarb said. "This is in part related to your brain increasing engagement of networks that track emotional intensity. So, if you are stressed out and trying to learn something new, it might help to think about exciting elements or strong feelings connected to what you are learning." The findings also point to a potentially useful insight about learning. Connecting information to something exciting, personally important, or emotionally engaging could make it easier to remember, particularly during stressful situations. Rather than simply disrupting memory, stress can sometimes help the brain identify which experiences deserve special attention and strengthen the networks involved in preserving them. Other Yale researchers involved in the study include Rajita Sinha, the Foundations Fund Endowed Professor in Psychiatry and professor in the Child Study Center and of neuroscience at Yale School of Medicine (YSM), and Todd Constable, the Elizabeth Mears and House Jameson Professor of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging and professor of neurosurgery at YSM. top.title: This bird flies thousands of miles, but its wings have a catch
top.summary: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected trade-off in the wings of the European nightjar, a bird that migrates thousands of kilometers but sacrifices high-speed flight efficiency to hunt insects with remarkable agility. Even more surprisingly, it generates thrust on the upward wingbeat, a technique that could inspire new flying technologies.
top.text: A bird that migrates thousands of miles has revealed a surprising secret about how wings work. Scientists have discovered that European nightjars sacrifice flight efficiency for agility and use an unexpected wingbeat technique previously associated mainly with bats and insects. The European nightjar ( Caprimulgus europaeus ) is a nighttime hunter that makes an extraordinary annual migration between Europe and southern Africa. Yet the wings that carry it across vast distances must also perform a very different task: helping the bird catch insects while flying slowly and making sharp turns. Scientists at Lund University have discovered that these competing demands come with a surprising trade-off. Although the nightjar is built to handle long migrations, its wings are not perfectly optimized for efficient flight at higher speeds. To investigate how nightjars fly, researchers studied the birds in a wind tunnel, recording their movements at different speeds and measuring the patterns of airflow left behind their wings. The experiments revealed that the nightjar's broad wing tips, which likely help it maneuver during slow flight, become a disadvantage as the bird flies faster. At higher speeds, its wings generate lift less efficiently. Lift is the aerodynamic force that helps keep a bird airborne. The findings challenge the assumption that birds traveling enormous distances must have wings optimized primarily for efficient long-distance flight. "This runs counter to the intuitive image of a long-distance migrant as a perfectly optimized flying machine. Instead, the nightjar's wings appear to be a compromise between several different demands. The bird can fly slowly and maneuver while hunting, but the trade-off is reduced efficiency in lift generation at higher speeds," says Christoffer Johansson, associate professor at Lund University. The researchers also uncovered another surprising feature of the nightjar's flight. Even as the bird raises its wings during the upward portion of each wingbeat, it continues to generate thrust, the force that helps propel it forward. This is unusual because such an active upward wing movement, known as an upstroke, has previously been linked mainly to the flight mechanics of bats and insects rather than birds. The discovery suggests that animals with very different evolutionary histories may have developed similar aerodynamic solutions to the challenges of flying. "What's interesting is that the same type of aerodynamic solution seems to appear in quite different animals. This suggests that the upstroke does not have to be merely a passive or lift generating part of the wingbeat. It can be actively used to generate thrust when the wings cannot be folded very much," says Christoffer Johansson. The results offer a broader lesson about how evolution shapes animals that depend on the same body structures for different activities. Rather than producing wings perfectly suited to one purpose, evolution can favor designs that balance several competing needs. For the nightjar, that means combining the ability to migrate across continents with the agility required to hunt insects at low speeds. Understanding these compromises could also lead to improvements in aviation technology, particularly drones and other robotic aircraft that use flapping wings. Like birds, these machines may face mechanical restrictions on how much their wings can fold during each wingbeat. Learning how nightjars generate thrust during the upstroke could help engineers develop more effective ways to move through the air. Researchers now hope to determine whether this unusual flight mechanism is widespread among other birds and flying animals or whether it represents a more specialized adaptation. "We now want to investigate how common this way of generating force is among other birds and flying animals. It could help us understand which aerodynamic principles are specific to the nightjar and which are more general. This knowledge may also inspire the development of new types of flapping aircraft," Christoffer Johansson concludes. Materials provided by Lund University . top.title: A 24-year study uncovers a surprising climate benefit beneath forests
top.summary: Scientists have discovered that some forest soils are becoming surprisingly better at removing methane from the atmosphere as temperatures rise and rainfall declines. A study spanning up to 24 years found methane absorption increasing by an average of 3% annually, challenging previous predictions about climate change's effects on forests.
top.text: Forest soils are playing a surprisingly powerful role in removing methane from the atmosphere, and new findings suggest that certain effects of climate change could make them even better at it. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming, but microorganisms living in the soil can break it down before it builds up in the air. Scientists from the University of Göttingen and the Baden-Württemberg Forest Research Institute (FVA) analyzed the world's most comprehensive collection of long-term measurements of methane absorption by forest soils. Their findings revealed an unexpected trend: under certain climate conditions that could become more common in the future, forest soils can actually increase the amount of methane they remove from the atmosphere. The researchers examined measurements collected from 13 forest sites in southwestern Germany over periods of up to 24 years. On average, the amount of methane absorbed by the soils increased by approximately 3% annually. The researchers linked this rise to declining rainfall and warmer temperatures, which create conditions that make it easier for methane to enter the soil and be broken down by microorganisms. The findings, published in Agricultural and Forest Meteorology , challenge previous research suggesting that climate change is generally reducing the ability of forest soils to absorb methane. To understand how methane absorption changes over time, the researchers examined an extensive collection of soil gas measurements gathered through the FVA's long-running monitoring program. The measurements included soil gas profiles, which reveal the chemical composition of gases trapped in the soil at different depths. Every two weeks, researchers collected air samples through thin tubes installed beneath the ground and analyzed them in a laboratory. This repeated sampling allowed scientists to track changes in methane concentrations over many years. To confirm their findings, the team also used an independent measurement technique involving airtight chambers placed directly on the soil surface. By monitoring how gas concentrations changed inside these chambers, the researchers could determine whether the soil was absorbing methane and calculate how much was being removed. Combining these methods gave the scientists a detailed picture of methane uptake across the forest sites and how it responded to changing environmental conditions. Although methane absorption varied considerably between the 13 locations, a clear overall pattern emerged. Forest soils in southwestern Germany were particularly effective at removing methane from the atmosphere during periods of lower rainfall and higher temperatures. "Our long-term data shows that climate change does not necessarily have a negative impact on how much methane forest soils absorb. While the largest study to date from the US found a decline in methane uptake of up to 80 percent due to increasing rainfall, our significantly more comprehensive field study in south-western Germany found the opposite, " explains Professor Martin Maier at Göttingen University's Department of Crop Sciences, who led the study and was previously involved in the FVA's soil gas monitoring program. "We observed a significant long-term increase in methane uptake in the forest areas we studied." The explanation lies partly in how water moves through the ground. When soil becomes saturated with moisture, water fills many of the tiny spaces between soil particles, making it more difficult for gases to move through them. Drier soil contains more pores filled with air, allowing atmospheric methane to travel deeper into the ground. Once methane enters the soil, microorganisms use it as an energy source, breaking it down in the process. Rising temperatures can slightly accelerate this microbial activity, allowing the organisms to consume methane more quickly. Together, these two effects help explain why warmer temperatures and reduced rainfall were associated with greater methane absorption in the forests studied. The results offer a different perspective from several major international research reviews. These analyses, known as meta-analyses, combine findings from numerous individual studies to identify broader patterns. Many have concluded that methane absorption by forest soils is declining. However, the German study suggests that the relationship between climate change and methane uptake is more complicated than those overall trends indicate. While increasing rainfall can reduce methane absorption by limiting the movement of gas through soil, drier conditions can produce the opposite effect. The findings do not mean that climate change is beneficial for forests overall. Instead, they demonstrate that its effects on methane absorption can differ considerably depending on local temperatures, rainfall patterns, and soil conditions. The researchers emphasize that these regional differences make long-term monitoring especially important. Shorter studies or analyses that combine measurements from widely different environments may miss gradual changes that only become apparent after years of observation. "Our results make it clear that taking a series of measurements over many years and running monitoring programs are indispensable for assessing the real effects of climate change," says Maier.
