top.title: First drug-focused guideline outlines newer treatments for primary biliary cholangitis
top.summary: For the first time, a joint guideline from the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) and American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) evaluates newer medications for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), the most common cholestatic disease in adults. Published in Gastroenterology and HEPATOLOGY, the guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for diagnosis and treatment.

top.title: Potassium binder may ease the burden of dietary potassium restriction in people on dialysis
top.summary: Dietary potassium restriction is important for managing hyperkalemia, or high blood potassium levels, in individuals on maintenance hemodialysis, but it imposes a substantial day-to-day burden. Results from a recent clinical trial indicate that adding the potassium binder sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) may help. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

top.title: Fruits and vegetables outperform medication for treating metabolic acidosis in chronic kidney disease
top.summary: In people with chronic kidney disease (CKD), oral sodium bicarbonate is a standard treatment for metabolic acidosis (too much acid buildup in the body), but results from a recent clinical trial indicate that dietary acid reduction with base-producing fruits and vegetables may be a better option. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

top.title: Liver tumors form without detectable driver mutations in mice, revealing epigenetic route
top.summary: Cancers can develop through epigenetic pathways even without driver gene mutations (DGMs), according to a study from Science Tokyo. Researchers uncovered the YAP1–TEAD–TET1 axis, which triggers DNA demethylation and activates multiple oncogenes in hepatocellular carcinoma. Suppressing TET1 reduced tumor formation in mice, while analysis of human liver disease data supported the relevance of these findings. This study reveals an alternative epigenetic route to cancer development and offers new insights into DGM-negative cancers.

top.title: How L-carnitine, found in red meat and exercise supplements, may amplify inflammation
top.summary: In a study published Oct. 19 in Cell, Yale researchers identified a previously unknown mechanism by which a nutrient abundant in red meat and commonly used in exercise supplements may amplify inflammation.

top.title: “Crawzilla” was huge. Then scientists found an even bigger crayfish
top.summary: A nationwide search for giant crayfish uncovered a record-breaking Tennessee specimen and a surprising mystery about how big these freshwater creatures can grow. Scientists found that North American crayfish seem to hit a biological size limit, possibly because of their muscles or protective shells.
top.text: A giant crayfish nicknamed "Crawzilla" has sparked an unexpected scientific discovery, revealing a possible biological limit to how large North America's crayfish can grow. The investigation began when Caitlin Bloomer pulled an enormous Crawzilla crawdad from the mud during a biological survey in Kentucky. Crawzilla is the creature's actual common name, and Bloomer was convinced she had captured the largest crayfish ever documented. But when she proudly showed her discovery to a colleague, the reaction was not quite what she expected. "I thought, 'There's no doubt I have caught the biggest crayfish anyone's ever seen!' I brought it back to campus to show my colleague, naturally bragging about having caught the biggest-ever crayfish. But, as all biologists and sport fishermen do, he took one look and said, 'No way, I've caught bigger,'" said Bloomer, a teaching assistant professor in the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Sciences within the College of Agricultural, Consumer and Environmental Sciences at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. What started as a little friendly rivalry soon turned into a nationwide search for record-breaking crayfish. Bloomer contacted biologists and museum curators across the country, asking them to examine their collections for unusually large specimens. Using calipers, instruments designed to measure objects with great precision, the researchers compared the sizes of preserved crayfish. Their search produced a list of 20 exceptionally large individuals representing 18 different species. The results were published in the scientific journal Ecology . Although Bloomer's original Crawzilla did not claim the top spot, it still earned a place among the largest specimens identified. "Mine was not the biggest, but it did make the top 20, so I'm super proud of it," Bloomer said. "And it was also the only burrowing crayfish to make the list, so I'll take the win." Scientists Identify the Largest Known North American Crayfish The biggest specimen belonged to a Tennessee bottlebrush crayfish preserved in the collection at West Liberty University in West Virginia. It measured an impressive 86.6 millimeters, or approximately 3.4 inches, excluding its tail, claws, and antennae. The record-holder was not a recent catch. It had been collected in 2011 by Dr. Zac Loughman and students from West Liberty University, making the discovery possible through the examination of existing museum specimens. "I knew we had some massive crayfish in the West Liberty University Astacology Collection, but it was a surprise to learn we had the two largest specimens known from North America! Our record-holder, a Tennessee bottlebrush crayfish collected by Dr. Zac Loughman and West Liberty students back in 2011, shows just how amazing and diverse crayfish can be," said Zackary Graham, an assistant professor of biology at West Liberty University. "Its carapace alone is about the length of a credit card, and with the tail and claws, it stretches nearly the width of a sheet of notebook paper. Both of these giants are now proudly displayed in my office, and I show them to just about everyone who walks in." Other institutions also contributed impressive specimens. The Illinois Natural History Survey, which belongs to the Prairie Research Institute at the University of Illinois, accounted for six of the 20 largest crayfish. The Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of Natural History contributed another four. Beyond settling the competition, the researchers uncovered a more intriguing scientific question. Their measurements provided some of the first estimates of the upper size limits for North American crayfish, and the results suggested that these animals may face a surprisingly consistent growth ceiling. Despite differences among species and environments, the largest individuals tended to reach roughly 80 millimeters in the body measurement used by the researchers. That raised an obvious question: Why do North American crayfish appear to stop growing at around this size when some species elsewhere in the world, including the Tasmanian giant freshwater crayfish, can become dramatically larger? "They all seemed to max out around that 80-millimeter mark, but we weren't sure why, especially given that there are absolutely massive crayfish in other parts of the world," Bloomer said. "We started looking at things like latitude, oxygen availability, and habitat type as possible correlates to explain why certain species and individuals were larger than others, but we weren't seeing any patterns." The team examined whether geographic location, oxygen levels, or the type of environment where a crayfish lives could explain why some grow larger than others. However, none of these factors showed a clear relationship with maximum body size. That unexpected result pointed the researchers toward a different possibility. Rather than being primarily controlled by environmental conditions, crayfish growth may be constrained by the animals' own biology. One potential explanation involves their exoskeletons, the hard outer coverings that protect their bodies. Differences in shell structure or muscle anatomy might impose physical limits on how large North American crayfish can become. For now, that remains a hypothesis. Further research will be needed to determine whether these biological features actually restrict their growth. "This was a case where we saw something unusual in the field and it sparked a future research direction," Bloomer said. "We think that it could really be worthwhile to look at the physiology of crayfish to see if something there is influencing their body size." Crayfish are familiar inhabitants of streams, rivers, and other freshwater environments. Many people encounter them as children, making them among the most recognizable aquatic animals in North America. Yet even with their widespread presence, scientists are still discovering basic facts about their biology, including how large they can grow and what determines their maximum size. "Anyone that goes to a stream as a kid knows what crayfish are -- they're almost a universal onboarding for people to care about aquatic life. I still go out with people who are in their 50s or 60s, who recall catching crawfish in the creek when they were seven," Bloomer said. "It's just amazing how much we still have to learn about them." Bloomer also emphasized that the investigation would not have been possible without museum collections. By comparing specimens preserved over many years, researchers were able to answer a fundamental question that would have been difficult to investigate through fieldwork alone. What began with one unusually large crayfish and a disagreement between colleagues has now opened a new line of scientific inquiry into the biological factors that shape the size of these familiar freshwater creatures. top.title: A forgotten fossil reveals a fearsome dinosaur with giant claws
top.summary: A 120-million-year-old fossil forgotten in a museum for nearly a century has revealed a terrifying new dinosaur that may have been more dangerous to humans than a T. rex. The tiger-sized predator also provides the first evidence of megaraptorans in Europe, helping explain how these mysterious dinosaurs eventually became gigantic hunters.
top.text: A dinosaur fossil that spent nearly a century overlooked in a museum collection has turned out to belong to an entirely new species of prehistoric predator. About the size of a large tiger and armed with enormous curved claws, the animal roamed what is now Britain approximately 120 million years ago. The discovery was made by researchers led by University College London (UCL), who examined a fossil skull fragment originally found on the Isle of Wight. Their findings, published in the journal Royal Society Open Science , identify the dinosaur as Invictibellatrix amberina , the first known European member of a mysterious group of carnivorous dinosaurs called megaraptorans. These agile predators walked on two legs and were closely related to tyrannosaurs, including the famous Tyrannosaurus rex . However, their hunting equipment was strikingly different. Rather than relying primarily on massive jaws, megaraptorans had relatively narrow skulls, powerful arms, and huge curved claws that helped them seize their prey. Some members of this group eventually became enormous predators, rivaling tyrannosaurs in size. Invictibellatrix , however, was among the earliest and smallest megaraptorans discovered so far. Its name translates to "unconquered female warrior," a reference to the powerful predators that later emerged from this evolutionary lineage. The fossil consists of part of the rear of the dinosaur's skull. Although the Natural History Museum acquired it in 1924, its scientific importance went unrecognized for generations. By comparing the fragment with fossils from related dinosaurs, researchers were able to estimate what this long-extinct animal might have looked like and how it lived. Lead author Dr. Cassius Morrison (UCL Earth Sciences) said: "Based on what we know about its closest relatives, Invictibellatrix would have been three to four meters long and just over a meter and a half in height -- about as tall as a human. It would likely have had feathers and its claws might have been about 10cm to 20cm long. It would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals -- occupying a similar role in the food chain to the hyena today. "It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex. We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small. "It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years. Lots of bones are found on the Isle of Wight -- who knows what else is waiting to be discovered." Although humans never encountered these dinosaurs, Morrison's comparison highlights an intriguing difference between predators of different sizes. A relatively small carnivore might have regarded a human as worthwhile prey, whereas an enormous hunter such as T. rex may have preferred much larger animals. Beyond identifying a previously unknown species, the fossil provides an important missing piece in the evolutionary history of megaraptorans. These dinosaurs remain among the least understood groups of large meat eaters because their fossils are exceptionally rare. Scientists have long suspected that they first evolved in Asia before spreading through Europe and eventually reaching the southern supercontinent of Gondwana (including present-day Africa, South America and Antarctica). There was one major problem with that explanation: Until now, no megaraptoran fossils had been identified in Europe. The discovery of Invictibellatrix provides the evidence researchers needed to support that proposed migration route. Co-author Charlie Scherer, a PhD student at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "This new species is the first proof we have that megaraptorans were also present in Europe and that they reached Gondwana this way rather than island-hopping further south." The finding suggests that Europe was an important part of the journey that eventually brought these predators to the southern continents, where some of their descendants became dominant hunters. To determine exactly what kind of dinosaur they were examining, the scientists used CT scanning technology to investigate the fossil in detail. The scans allowed them to build a three-dimensional reconstruction of the skull fragment, along with a model of its internal cavity. This provided clues about the shape of the space that once housed the dinosaur's brain. The team then compared its anatomy with fossils from several other groups of meat-eating dinosaurs, including tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs, raptors, and other predators that walked on two legs. Several unusual features helped distinguish the specimen from known species. These included an oval opening where the spinal cord connected to the brain and a distinctive crest shaped like an hourglass. Together, these anatomical characteristics indicated that the fossil represented a previously unidentified dinosaur. The researchers also used computer algorithms to compare its skeletal features with those of other dinosaurs. These analyses consistently placed Invictibellatrix within the megaraptoran group, providing further support for the identification. The team went beyond examining the fossil itself, using mathematical models to reconstruct how megaraptorans spread and evolved over millions of years. Their analysis combined the available fossil record with evolutionary relationships among dinosaurs, ancient geography, and climate conditions. The results suggest that megaraptorans were distributed widely around the world during the Early Cretaceous (i.e., at the time of Invictibellatrix ). However, their fortunes appear to have changed dramatically as the Cretaceous continued. By the Late Cretaceous, tens of millions of years later, megaraptorans had probably disappeared from the northern supercontinent of Laurasia (including modern-day Europe). In the south, the story was very different. Megaraptorans continued evolving across Gondwana, eventually becoming some of the largest and most formidable predators in their ecosystems. Some developed claws measuring up to 35cm (14") long. One particularly impressive example, Maip macrothorax , lived in what is now Argentina and is estimated to have reached nine to 10 meters in length, with a body weight comparable to that of an elephant. Exactly why megaraptorans apparently vanished from northern regions remains uncertain. The researchers suggest several possibilities, including changes in climate, shifts in environmental conditions, and competition from other large carnivorous dinosaurs such as tyrannosaurs. The fossil that made this discovery possible was originally collected by amateur paleontologist Reginald Walter Tooley near the base of a cliff on the southwestern coast of the Isle of Wight. Tooley discovered more than 1,000 fossil specimens during his lifetime. Following his death, the Natural History Museum acquired his collection, including the skull fragment that would eventually be identified as Invictibellatrix . The discovery highlights how important fossils can remain unrecognized even after spending decades in museum collections. Professor Paul Barrett, the study's senior author from the Natural History Museum, said: "Despite over 200 years of collecting, the Isle of Wight continues to surprise us with new dinosaur species, and finds of carnivorous dinosaurs, such as Invictibellatrix, have been particularly elusive. "Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made." The researchers also gave the dinosaur's name a deeper meaning. In their paper, they explained that Invictibellatrix was chosen to "give hope and strength to all those who are bullied, discriminated, victimized, and oppressed that tomorrow will be theirs and not to give up in face of such odds." top.title: Stanford’s new microscope reveals living cells like never before
top.summary: Stanford scientists have developed a revolutionary microscope that reveals the hidden inner workings of living cells in real time, without the fluorescent labels that can interfere with observations. The breakthrough could provide new insights into cancer, infectious diseases, and how drugs interact with cells.
top.text: A new microscope developed at Stanford University allows scientists to watch the tiny structures inside living cells move and interact in real time, providing an exceptionally detailed view without the fluorescent labels typically used to make these structures visible. Researchers at Stanford have created a powerful new imaging system that reveals the inner workings of living cells with remarkable clarity. By combining two advanced microscopy techniques, the instrument achieves a resolution of approximately 120 nanometers, an unprecedented level of detail for an approach that does not require fluorescent labels. Known as Interferometric Image Scanning Microscopy (iISM), the technology makes it possible to observe multiple cellular structures simultaneously while they move, change, and respond to their surroundings. Scientists can also investigate what happens when cells encounter drugs or disease causing organisms, potentially uncovering biological processes that have been difficult to study. The breakthrough, described in the Nature portfolio journal Light: Science and Applications , could lead to advances in cancer research, drug development, infectious disease studies, and investigations of how plants interact with microorganisms. "This new microscope provides a fantastic new view into the cell, where you can see the tiny structures and machines in the cell moving, changing, and interacting without having to add fluorescence to observe them," said senior author W.E. Moerner, the Harry S. Mosher Professor of Chemistry in Stanford's School of Humanities and Sciences. "It's a wonderful look into these complex little cellular boxes that drive our life." One of the most important advantages of the new microscope is its ability to reveal cellular activity without relying on fluorescent markers. Many existing microscopy techniques use fluorescent substances to highlight specific structures inside cells. Although these methods have transformed biological research, they come with limitations. Researchers can generally label only a small number of structures at once, making it difficult to observe how different components interact across an entire cell. Fluorescent signals can also fade during observation through a process known as photobleaching. In addition, introducing the labels can be challenging, and some markers may alter the behavior of the very structures scientists want to study. The Stanford system avoids these problems by imaging cells without fluorescent labels. This allows researchers to follow numerous cellular components over extended periods while observing their activity in a more natural setting. Another advantage is that iISM requires substantially less illumination power than comparable label-free methods that produce high-contrast images. Lower light exposure reduces the possibility of photodamage, which occurs when the light used for imaging harms living cells or interferes with their normal functions. Although other specialized microscopes can achieve finer resolution, the combination of detailed imaging, gentle illumination, and extended observation makes iISM particularly valuable for studying living biological systems. The researchers emphasize that their technology is intended to complement fluorescence microscopy rather than replace it. First author Michelle Kueppers, a postdoctoral scholar in Moerner's laboratory, explained that combining the strengths of different imaging approaches could help scientists answer previously inaccessible questions. "Every method has its advantages and disadvantages, and we believe in a complementary implementation in the future," Kueppers said. "If we use the strengths of fluorescence for molecular specificity and the strength of iISM for label-free context and dynamics, we can really start tackling questions that have been difficult to address before." The breakthrough comes from bringing together two different microscopy technologies, each with its own advantages. Moerner received the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his pioneering contributions to super-resolution fluorescence microscopy. He specifically recruited Kueppers to Stanford because of her doctoral research involving a technique called "interferometric scattering microscopy." This method relies on a familiar property of light: scattering. Light changes direction when it encounters tiny particles. The same basic phenomenon explains why the sky appears blue. As sunlight passes through Earth's atmosphere, molecules, dust, and water droplets scatter its different wavelengths. Shorter blue wavelengths scatter more strongly than longer red wavelengths, producing the blue color we see overhead. Interferometric scattering microscopy takes advantage of this behavior on a much smaller scale. A laser illuminates a cell, causing tiny structures inside it to scatter some of the incoming light. Because the scattered signal is extremely weak, a second laser beam is used to amplify it through interference, allowing the microscope to detect structures that would otherwise be difficult to observe. The Stanford team improved this approach by combining it with technology adapted from advanced confocal microscopes. Traditional confocal microscopes use a small opening called a pinhole and a single detector to isolate light from a selected area. More advanced versions replace that arrangement with camera-based detector arrays capable of collecting multiple views of the same region. The researchers incorporated an array detector into their new microscope, allowing it to collect more light than a conventional system built around a pinhole and single detector. The advantage of collecting multiple perspectives is similar to the way human vision works. Our two eyes observe the world from slightly different positions, helping the brain distinguish nearby objects from those farther away. The Stanford microscope uses a related principle, but instead of relying on just two perspectives, its detector array gathers tens to hundreds of views. The researchers developed a computational method that combines these measurements to generate images with improved sharpness, contrast, depth information, and precision. By merging the strengths of interferometric scattering microscopy and advanced detector arrays, the team created an instrument capable of resolving structures as small as approximately 120 nanometers. For perspective, a nanometer is one billionth of a meter. At this scale, researchers can examine extremely small cellular structures and follow their movements and interactions. Crucially, the microscope achieves this resolution without sacrificing imaging speed or requiring intense laser illumination. Scientists can therefore observe living cells for longer periods while minimizing the risk of disturbing or damaging them. Moerner and Kueppers are continuing to refine the instrument, with the goal of eventually making it accessible to scientists across many areas of biology. Three collaborations with other Stanford research groups are already underway or in development, demonstrating the range of questions the technology could help investigate. One project uses the microscope to observe interactions among plant cells, fungi, and bacteria as they happen. By watching these organisms interact in real time, researchers hope to gain a clearer understanding of the complex relationships between plants and microbes. Another collaboration focuses on cancer treatment. Scientists are using iISM to investigate how a cancer drug enters a cell, potentially providing valuable information about how medications interact with their targets. A third project, still in the planning stages, will examine how red blood cells change shape when exposed to malaria infection. Observing these physical changes could offer new insights into how the disease affects blood cells. top.title: A 47-year study reveals the age when your body starts losing strength
top.summary: A 47-year study has uncovered a surprising turning point in physical aging: fitness and strength begin declining around age 35, even among people who exercise regularly. Researchers found that this decline accelerates as people get older, but starting to exercise in adulthood can still improve physical performance.
top.text: Aging may begin to affect your physical abilities earlier than you expect. A remarkable 47-year Swedish study found that fitness, muscle endurance, and physical performance generally begin declining around age 35, even among people who remain active. But the findings also offer an encouraging message. Although exercise cannot completely prevent the physical changes associated with aging, becoming more active during adulthood can still produce meaningful improvements in fitness and strength. Researchers at Karolinska Institutet in Sweden spent nearly five decades tracking how people's physical abilities changed as they grew older. Their findings, published in 2025 in the Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle , help explain when physical decline begins, how it progresses, and why staying active remains important throughout life. The research was part of the Swedish Physical Activity and Fitness study (SPAF), which followed 427 randomly selected men and women born in 1958. Participants underwent physical assessments over 47 years, beginning at age 16 and continuing through age 63. Unlike most earlier research on physical aging, which compared people of different ages at a single point in time, this project repeatedly examined the same individuals as they grew older. That distinction matters because physical abilities vary considerably from person to person. Following individuals over decades allowed researchers to observe how fitness changed within the same population rather than relying on comparisons between different generations. The assessments included aerobic fitness, muscular endurance, and muscle power. Aerobic fitness describes how effectively the body uses oxygen during exercise, while muscular endurance measures how long muscles can continue working. Muscle power reflects the ability to produce force quickly, which is important for activities such as jumping, climbing stairs, and maintaining mobility. The results revealed a consistent pattern. Aerobic fitness and muscular endurance generally reached their highest levels between ages 26 and 36, with physical performance beginning to decline around the mid-30s. Some abilities, particularly explosive muscle power, peaked even earlier. The decline was initially modest but became progressively faster with age. By age 63, average performance across the measurements had fallen by roughly 30 to 48 percent from peak levels. Importantly, the pattern appeared in both men and women. Although individual fitness levels differed, the overall rates of age-related decline were similar between the sexes. One of the most striking findings was that regular physical activity did not entirely prevent the decline associated with aging. Even people who remained physically active showed evidence of diminishing performance as they grew older. However, exercise made an important difference in how well people maintained their abilities. Participants who became physically active during adulthood experienced improvements in physical capacity of approximately 5 to 10 percent. Those who were already active during adolescence also tended to maintain better fitness, endurance, and muscle power throughout adulthood. These findings suggest that physical decline is not simply the result of becoming less active with age. Biological changes also appear to contribute, although exercise can help reduce their impact. "It is never too late to start moving. Our study shows that physical activity can slow the decline in performance, even if it cannot completely stop it. Now we will look for the mechanisms behind why everyone reaches their peak performance at age 35 and why physical activity can slow performance loss but not completely halt it," says Maria Westerståhl, lecturer at the Department of Laboratory Medicine and lead author of the study. The distinction is important. Reaching an average physical peak in the mid-30s does not mean everyone suddenly becomes weaker at that age. People can continue improving their individual fitness and strength through training, even after the age when population averages begin to decline. Scientists are still investigating exactly why physical performance begins deteriorating relatively early in adulthood. Several biological processes are thought to contribute. As people age, changes in muscle cells, the nervous system, and the body's ability to produce energy can gradually reduce physical performance. One possible contributor involves mitochondria, the tiny structures inside cells that convert nutrients into usable energy. Changes in mitochondrial function may affect how efficiently muscles produce the energy required for movement. Over time, muscles can also lose mass and become less responsive to the signals that trigger growth and repair. More advanced muscle deterioration can contribute to sarcopenia, an age-related condition involving the loss of muscle strength and mass that can make everyday activities increasingly difficult. Although these processes often become more noticeable later in life, the Swedish findings suggest that some underlying changes in physical function begin decades earlier. The researchers hope to determine which biological mechanisms drive this decline and why physical activity can delay, but not completely prevent, the loss of performance. The importance of maintaining physical fitness throughout adulthood extends beyond muscle strength. In a 2026 follow-up study published in Scientific Reports , researchers examined additional health outcomes using the same Swedish cohort. They found that people with better aerobic fitness at ages 34 and 52 tended to have less arterial stiffness at age 63. Arterial stiffness occurs when blood vessels become less flexible, making it harder for them to expand and contract as blood moves through the body. Greater stiffness is associated with increased cardiovascular risk. Notably, the relationship between earlier fitness and later artery health remained significant even after accounting for several established cardiovascular risk factors, including obesity, smoking, and blood pressure. The results do not establish that better fitness directly prevented arterial stiffening. However, they suggest that maintaining aerobic capacity during early and middle adulthood may have benefits that extend well into later life. Other research has reinforced the idea that exercise remains valuable even when physical performance inevitably declines with age. A 2026 study published in GeroScience followed 82 older adults who continued cycling over a nine-year period. Despite maintaining active lifestyles, participants experienced an average 19.7 percent decline in peak aerobic capacity. Yet their fitness remained remarkably high. Nearly all participants who completed the exercise test performed at or above the 90th percentile for their age when compared with reference populations. The findings suggest that although regular exercise cannot eliminate biological aging, it can help people maintain unusually high levels of physical function as they get older. Another 2026 study in The American Journal of Medicine followed 49 men ages 60 to 82 who had not previously participated in structured exercise training. Over four years, participants who performed weekly resistance exercises improved their upper and lower body strength. Those who combined resistance training with aerobic exercise also improved their aerobic fitness. Although the study was relatively small and participants chose their training programs, its findings support the idea that meaningful physical improvements remain possible well into older adulthood. The original Swedish research is continuing, with investigators planning another round of assessments when participants reach age 68. top.title: Scientists discover a surprising danger in smaller cancer cells
top.summary: Scientists have discovered that unusually small cancer cells carrying extra chromosomes can be far more aggressive than larger ones, growing faster, spreading more readily, and resisting common treatments. The surprising finding could help explain why some tumors are especially dangerous and provide a new way to predict cancer outcomes.
top.text: Some cancers grow faster, spread more aggressively, and respond less effectively to treatment than others. Researchers at Virginia Tech are uncovering surprising reasons behind these differences, including how abnormal cancer cells recruit healthy tissue to support tumor growth and why the size of certain cancer cells could help predict their danger. The discoveries emerged from years of painstaking laboratory work, including the careful examination of tumors grown in mice. Graduate student Megan Sweet, who studies biological sciences at Virginia Tech, spends much of her time preparing extremely thin slices of tumor tissue. Working inside a refrigerated metal chamber, she carefully adjusts a mounted tumor, roughly the size of a pinkie fingernail, toward a sharp cutting blade. "It's all about fine-tuning and making sure it's going to be an even slice," said Sweet, who studies biological sciences. As the blade moves through the tissue, it produces a steady, rhythmic chopping sound. "This is the hardest and most time-consuming part," Sweet said. "But it's also kind of meditative." Each section is cut so thin that light can pass through it. Sweet carefully transfers the delicate tissue onto a glass slide, where selected cellular structures are stained to make them easier to distinguish under a powerful microscope. The process involves repeated rounds of cutting, staining, examining, and comparing samples. Although painstaking, this work is helping scientists piece together why certain tumors become much more dangerous than others. The Virginia Tech team has published findings that shed new light on how cancer develops and progresses. Their research was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , with additional findings published earlier this year in Cancer Research . Most healthy cells in the human body are diploid, meaning they contain two complete sets of chromosomes, with one inherited from each parent. Under normal conditions, these cells divide to produce new cells with the same chromosome arrangement. Occasionally, however, something goes wrong during division, leaving cells with an abnormal number of chromosomes. When these errors are passed on during subsequent cell divisions, they can accumulate over time. Such changes are one of the ways cancer can develop. For the past five years, Sweet and fellow graduate student Mat Bloomfield have worked with cell biologist Daniela Cimini to investigate cells carrying abnormal numbers of chromosomes, a common characteristic of cancer. To study the consequences of these abnormalities, Cimini's team manipulated diploid cancer cells so they would duplicate their chromosomes without completing cell division. The result was a type of cell known as a tetraploid cell, which contains four complete sets of chromosomes rather than the usual two. These cells are not limited to laboratory experiments. Tetraploid cells can also emerge during the development of human tumors, and their presence has been associated with cancer progression and poorer outcomes for patients. Scientists have long recognized that tetraploid cells can make tumors more aggressive. What remained unclear was exactly how they contributed to cancer growth. To investigate, Sweet and Bloomfield compared tumors that developed from ordinary diploid cancer cells with those formed from tetraploid cancer cells. As tumors grew in mice, the proportion of tetraploid cells actually decreased. Despite this decline, the tumors continued expanding rapidly and reached substantial sizes. The researchers discovered that tetraploid cancer cells were encouraging the recruitment of stromal cells, which are noncancerous connective tissue cells that help provide structural support. These additional cells appeared to create an environment that favored further tumor development. "The presence of even a small fraction of these tetraploid cells can promote the recruitment of extra non-cancerous cells that support further tumor progression," Sweet said. The finding revealed a previously unrecognized mechanism through which abnormal cancer cells can promote tumor growth, even when they account for only a small portion of the tumor. A separate investigation uncovered another unexpected connection between tetraploid cells and cancer aggressiveness. Bloomfield was initially examining the physical characteristics of tetraploid cells. After producing tetraploid cells from human cancer cells and establishing colonies derived from individual cells, he noticed that the resulting groups were not all the same size. Because tetraploid cells contain twice the usual number of chromosome sets, the researchers expected them to be approximately twice as large as diploid cells. Instead, some of the cells were 25 to 30 percent smaller than anticipated. Even more surprisingly, those smaller cells proved to be more capable of forming aggressive tumors than their larger counterparts. "The smaller clones are more aggressive," Bloomfield said. "They grow faster, are more invasive, and more tolerant of common anti-cancer and stress-inducing drugs." Further experiments in mice supported these observations. Tumors containing smaller tetraploid cells frequently grew more quickly than those containing larger ones. The pattern was not restricted to a single type of cancer. Researchers observed similar results in both colorectal and breast cancer cells, suggesting that the relationship between tetraploid cell size and tumor aggressiveness may extend across different cancers. The researchers next examined whether the same relationship could be found in human cancers. They analyzed information from the Cancer Genome Atlas, a large collection of detailed data from thousands of cancer patient samples. The results revealed that smaller tetraploid cells were associated with worse prognoses and lower survival rates across several cancer types. This suggests that measuring the size of these abnormal cells could provide valuable information about how aggressively a tumor might behave. "We already knew that tetraploidy can make cells more tumorigenic, but now we know that if you incorporate the size of the cells, it can be more predictive of tumorigenic potential," Cimini said. The findings add an important dimension to scientists' understanding of cancer. Abnormal chromosome numbers have long been linked to dangerous tumor behavior, but the new research indicates that cell size may offer additional clues about a cancer's potential to grow and spread. The team now plans to investigate the biological mechanisms responsible for these effects in greater detail while continuing to examine human cancer data. For Sweet, that means more hours at the laboratory bench, carefully cutting and analyzing tiny sections of tumor tissue in the search for answers to one of cancer biology's most important questions. top.title: Legal encounters may offer overlooked opportunities for suicide prevention, analysis suggests
top.summary: Picture a forlorn man walking into a lawyer's office after his marriage has collapsed. The bank is threatening foreclosure, and his finances are in tatters. His problems may be legal on paper, but in person they can look far more complicated: panic, shame or the numb resignation of someone who can no longer imagine a way out. He did not come for counseling, and his lawyer is not a therapist. Still, the attorney may be sitting beside him at the worst moment of his life—with a chance to help before despair slides into tragedy.

top.title: Illegal fishing is thriving in African waters—a satellite system could help change that
top.summary: A patrol boat off the coast of Gabon intercepted three trawlers in July 2026, inside the Grand Sud Reserve. This is one of West and Central Africa's largest marine reserves, where industrial trawling is banned. None of the trawlers held a valid license. The patrol found them because analysts at the nonprofit Global Fishing Watch had studied satellite data and worked out where to look.

top.title: Hypnosis may help relieve stomach pain
top.summary: Stomach pain and other gastrointestinal complaints are common among children and adolescents. When symptoms recur over a long period, the cause may be a form of DGBI (disorders of gut-brain interaction), in which communication between the brain and the gut does not function as it should. This can affect both intestinal motility and the way pain is perceived.

top.title: Childhood adversity patterns reveal different links to hopelessness and drug or alcohol cravings
top.summary: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are known to increase the risk of substance use problems later in life. New research from George Mason University's College of Public Health suggests that the specific types of adversity a young person faces may be associated with different vulnerabilities to those risks.

top.title: FDA patient, consumer reps often tied to pharma-funded groups
top.summary: Patient and consumer representatives advising U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) expert panels might actually be a Trojan horse for the pharmaceutical industry, a new study says.

top.title: Horror’s monsters find new meaning with queer and trans audiences – how ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ dissects identity
top.summary: Horror as a genre has traditionally been rife with transphobia and homophobia. But LGBTQ+ fans love it anyway.
top.text: Queer horror is having a moment. The recent film “ Leviticus ” (2026), a harrowing allegory for conversion therapy , was a critical hit. Meanwhile, Ryan Murphy’s undeniably gay “ American Horror Story ” returned to TV this fall, offering a campier approach to the genre. But queer people’s fascination with horror is by no means new. For trans and queer viewers, horror has long acted as a mirror to reflect on complex personal questions of identity and embodiment. Another new film, Jane Schoenbrun’s “ Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma ” (2026), explores queer people’s relationship with horror. Schoenbrun’s film isn’t really a horror movie; it’s a movie about horror movies . The protagonist, a young auteur named Kris, is rebooting an old slasher franchise, “Camp Miasma.” The franchise has aged poorly, and she wants to update the film for a contemporary audience. “This part’s transphobic!” Kris mutters while watching the original film. But Kris is also helplessly obsessed with “Camp Miasma,” and Schoenbrun’s film suggests that it’s precisely the slasher’s troubling, problematic elements that have enthralled her. As both a trans studies scholar and a longtime horror fan, I know how she feels. In fact, Kris’ complicated relationship with “Camp Miasma” may feel deeply familiar for many queer and trans viewers. Horror has produced some of the most objectionable queer- and trans-coded characters in cinema history. These portrayals of LGBTQ+ people as monstrous and pathological can be found in films ranging from the low-budget slashers that inspired Schoenbrun – most notably “ Sleepaway Camp ” (1983) – to Oscar winners such as “ The Silence of the Lambs ” (1991). Yet queer and trans audiences have often found themselves strangely drawn to these films and to the horror genre overall . Why does a genre that has treated LGBTQ+ people so poorly keep them coming back? No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone. ‘Heartstopper’ is helping LGBTQ+ fans find hope and community across time and space Childhood experiences of LGBTQ+ stigma can harm romantic relationships decades later – psychologists explain how to reconnect with yourself and your partner Heated Rivalry shows how queer joy can disrupt hockey’s culture of masculinity Queerness is baked into the very structure of the horror genre. Film scholar Robin Wood summarized the horror formula as “Normality is threatened by the Monster.” As Wood points out, the social order that represents “normality” is often tied to heteronormative structures like the nuclear family and the heterosexual couple. Horror stages gleeful attacks on this order: Think of the family under siege by malevolent spirits, or the straight camp counselors hacked to bits after having sex. Such themes may resonate strongly for queers who find their goals and desires in tension with a society primarily built around cisgender, heterosexual life paths. Beyond its social elements, horror also offers queer and trans people a personal encounter with an aspect of themselves that they may find confusing or even upsetting: their bodies. Feminist scholar Carol Clover argued that horror is a “ body genre ,” meaning it is intended to activate a bodily response in the viewer. Often, one of the ways horror elicits this physical response is through the visceral, violent onscreen deformation of bodies. In body horror , the human body is depicted as an unruly, often disgusting and always vulnerable accumulation of flesh , blood and guts. Such images can mirror and affirm the difficult feelings that many queer and trans folks have experienced with regard to embodiment, their distress surrounding the forms their bodies take or the desires they feel. Horror’s depiction of monsters and monstrous bodies have allowed many queer and trans people to take ownership over their experiences of personal pain and social stigma. As trans theorist Susan Stryker put it, “I want to lay claim to the dark power of my monstrous identity without using it as a weapon against others or being wounded by it myself.” Other queer and trans writers, however, have asked about the limits of identifying with monstrosity. “How does building an identity on reclaiming the boogeyman affect the psyche ?” wonders critic Grace Byron. Horror, after all, centers on violence, brutality, fear and even death. Identifying with these forces might feel powerful in the moment, but it doesn’t necessarily help reckon with the real violence that led LGBTQ+ people to identify with them in the first place. When I teach horror , my students and I talk about how we might approach some of the most transphobic figures in the horror canon. Instead of identifying with these “monsters,” we try to think critically about the conditions that created them. Take the trans-coded serial killer Buffalo Bill, from “The Silence of the Lambs.” Scholar Cael Keegan argues that “The Silence of the Lambs” raises issues of state violence against transgender people. Similarly, scholar Grace Lavery reads Buffalo Bill as a victim of medical gatekeeping , which bars lifesaving gender-related care from those who need it. Rather than either rejecting characters like Buffalo Bill or embracing their monstrosity, queer viewers and their allies could instead ask what these characters show about the structural conditions that keep queer and trans people at the margins of society. When my students approach horror, I encourage them to consider the strategy that queer theorist José Esteban Muñoz offers for minority groups engaging with harmful representations in dominant culture: disidentification . For Muñoz, to “disidentify” means refusing to see yourself in images that degrade you, yet still finding ways of making those violent representations generative for your own thinking, dreaming and living. “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” is about disidentifying with horror. It acknowledges the harmful, long-standing transphobia of the genre. And it is also frank about the disturbing prevalence of sexual violence in horror, both onscreen and behind the scenes . But the queer characters in “Camp Miasma” – both in Schoenbrun’s film and in its fictional counterpart – still manage to connect with themselves and their bodies. And I think they do this not just by watching horror, but by watching themselves watch horror. So perhaps the draw of horror for queer and trans people isn’t just that it lets them identify with onscreen monsters or victims of violence. It’s that it gives them the opportunity to reflect on these identifications – and to reject them or transform them. In the process of finding meaning in horror’s monstrous worlds, queer and trans people tap into their own power to respond to the monstrous world around them.
